situation: A block is being implemented bottom-up or hierarchically; the chip-level or parent-level timing budget must be translated into set_input_delay / set_output_delay at the block's ports so the block's internal implementation tool knows how much combinational time it is allowed to consume.
derivation: Start from the launching register's clock period T. Reserve a portion of T for the upstream block's clock-to-output plus interconnect (call it D_upstream), and a portion for the downstream capture block's setup plus interconnect (D_downstream). The block's internal budget is T − D_upstream − D_downstream − T_setup_margin. Express D_upstream as set_input_delay -max on the block's input port (referenced to the block's clock), and D_downstream as set_output_delay -max on the block's output port. Always pair -max (for setup) with -min (for hold): set_input_delay -min models the earliest upstream launch; set_output_delay -min models the earliest the downstream can accept data. Skipping -min leaves hold unconstrained on boundary paths. A common starting heuristic when nothing else is known is input delay ≈ 40% of T, output delay ≈ 40% of T, leaving ~20% for internal logic — but this must be refined against real upstream/downstream models. For a 2-cycle multicycle path crossing the boundary, the block-level constraint inherits the multicycle: set_input_delay 5 -clock clk [get_ports IN]; set_multicycle_path 2 -setup -through IN -to dest_reg/D — the available budget becomes 2T − input_delay − output_delay.
wrong_way: Engineer copies the chip-level period straight into the block as if the block owns the whole period (set_input_delay 0, set_output_delay 0). The block optimizes as if it has T ns, but in reality upstream already consumed part of T and downstream needs part of T; at chip integration the path is over budget and cannot be closed. The inverse error is over-reserving (input_delay + output_delay > T) which makes the block unimplementable and pushes the failure back to the top level with no recourse.
defense: Justify the split with the chip-level timing budget spreadsheet: show D_upstream from the driving block's CTS/STA report, D_downstream from the capturing block's required setup plus estimated interconnect, and the residual left for the block under review. In review, present the equation T = D_upstream + D_internal + D_downstream + T_setup_margin and demonstrate each term. If a multicycle path crosses the boundary, show the originating chip-level set_multicycle_path and the derived block-level exception.
signoff_risk: Too tight (input_delay + output_delay reserved too much): the block fails internal timing, wasting area/power trying to meet an impossible budget, and may force an expensive block re-floorplan. Too loose (reserved too little): the block closes locally but at chip-level integration the path is out of budget; the violation surfaces late, after both blocks are frozen, and can only be patched with an ECO or a frequency reduction. Either direction is expensive at signoff — tight constraints cost implementation effort, loose constraints cost integration schedule.

situation: Two adjacent blocks A→B are both still in early implementation; neither has a final netlist, but the chip-level timing budget must be partitioned so each team has a target. The interface is bidirectional or multi-bit.
derivation: Partition the available period T based on relative complexity and known hard limits, not equally. Estimate each block's rough logic depth (number of stages, type of logic) and assign D_A_internal and D_B_internal proportionally. Then derive: set_output_delay on A's output port = D_B_internal + D_downstream_capture + margin; set_input_delay on B's input port = D_A_internal + D_upstream_launch + margin. A practical rule: give the harder block more of the period. If A is a simple pipeline stage and B contains a complex ALU, reserve maybe 20% of T for A's internal delay and 60% for B's, with 20% for clock uncertainties and wiring. Document the assumption explicitly: 'B assumed to need 3 logic levels, A assumed 1'. As each block matures, re-derive the boundary constraints from actual STA data and iterate.
wrong_way: Splitting the period 50/50 regardless of block complexity, or worse, each block owner independently assuming they have the full period minus a token reservation. When both blocks come back over budget on the shared interface, there is no slack left to trade and the chip frequency must be lowered. Another common error: forgetting that output delay on A is the same physical constraint as input delay on B — defining them inconsistently (different clocks, different margins) creates a contradictory budget that neither side can meet.
defense: Present the partition as a 2-variable equation with the sum constrained to T. Show the logic-level estimate for each block and the rationale for the asymmetric split. Get both block owners to sign off on the numbers. Use a central budget document that is version-controlled and updated as blocks mature.
signoff_risk: Too tight on one block: that block cannot close and demands the other block give back budget, triggering a cross-team negotiation late in the schedule. Too loose: the block over-optimizes (area/power penalty) but the true risk is that the 'loose' block's actual delay at maturity exceeds the optimistic reservation, blowing the interface budget with no slack to recover. At signoff, an interface that was never jointly validated against real netlists is a classic source of last-minute frequency cuts.

pattern_name: Virtual clock for off-chip I/O timing
situation: Data enters or leaves the chip synchronized to a clock that is not present as a port on the chip (e.g., a board-level clock driving an external device, or the chip's own input clock after board-level delay). set_input_delay / set_output_delay must reference a clock, but that clock has no on-chip node.
derivation: Create a virtual clock with the same period and waveform as the external reference: create_clock -period 10 -name virt_clk. Then constrain I/O relative to it: set_input_delay -clock virt_clk -max 3.5 [get_ports data_in]; set_input_delay -clock virt_clk -min 0.1 [get_ports data_in]; set_output_delay -clock virt_clk -max 4.0 [get_ports data_out]; set_output_delay -clock virt_clk -min 0.3 [get_ports data_out]. The -max models latest arrival (setup) and -min models earliest arrival (hold). For a pure combinational pad-to-pad path, the constraint is: input_delay_value + max feedthrough delay + output_delay_value = virt_clk period. The virtual clock isolates the I/O timing from the on-chip clock tree latency and uncertainty, giving a clean reference. Its period must match the external device's clock; if the external clock is 100 MHz, the virtual clock period is 10 ns.
wrong_way: Referencing the on-chip clock (e.g., the clock after the input buffer) for input/output delays. This drags the input buffer delay and on-chip clock tree latency into the I/O budget, making the constraint unrealistically tight. Alternatively, omitting -min: only specifying -max gives hold analysis no bound, leaving hold unconstrained and risking hold violations that surface only at signoff or in silicon. A third error: using different virtual clock periods for input vs output when both reference the same external clock — the round-trip budget becomes inconsistent.
defense: Show the board-level timing diagram: the external clock's relationship to data at the chip ball. Demonstrate that the virtual clock period equals the external clock period. Present the input delay as the sum of external device Tco + board trace delay + package delay; output delay as board trace + downstream device setup. If the on-chip clock has extra latency or uncertainty, explain why the virtual clock (without those) is the correct reference.
signoff_risk: Too tight (input_delay or output_delay over-estimated): the I/O buffers and internal logic are over-optimized, costing power and area; or the path fails to close and the interface frequency must drop. Too loose (under-estimated delays): at silicon, the external device misses setup or hold — the interface is flaky or dead. This class of error is especially nasty because it may pass STA but fail on the board due to the optimistic board-model assumptions baked into the virtual clock.

pattern_name: Generated clock from divider / PLL / mux
situation: An internal clock is produced by a divide-by-N register, a PLL/MMCM, or a clock mux. STA must understand the relationship between this generated clock and its source to correctly time paths that cross between them.
derivation: Use create_generated_clock with -source pointing to a physical pin or port (never a clock name), and specify the relationship: -divide_by N, -multiply_by M, -edges {…}, or -invert. For a divide-by-2 from a flop: create_generated_clock -name clk_div2 -source [get_pins div_reg/CK] -divide_by 2 [get_pins div_reg/Q]. For a PLL output: create_generated_clock -name clk_150 -source [get_pins pll/CLKIN] -multiply_by 3 -divide_by 2 [get_pins pll/CLKOUT]. The -source must be the master clock's physical origin (e.g., the CK pin of the divider flop, or the input of the PLL), not an arbitrary node. If the generated clock passes through a mux with multiple sources, each source needs its own create_generated_clock with -add and -master_clock to model all possible waveforms. The timing tool then computes latency and waveform propagation from master to generated clock automatically.
wrong_way: Leaving the generated clock unconstrained — the tool treats it as asynchronous to its source, producing spurious cross-domain violations or, worse, missing real timing relationships. Or pointing -source to the wrong node (e.g., the generated clock's own output pin instead of the master source), which breaks the waveform derivation. Or using create_clock instead of create_generated_clock, severing the link to the master and hiding the true phase/frequency relationship. Another subtle error: when a mux selects between two clock sources, defining only one generated clock — paths under the unmodeled source become untimed.
defense: In review, display the clock tree: master clock → generating cell → generated clock. Show the -source argument resolves to a real physical pin. For dividers, prove the divide ratio matches the RTL. For PLLs, cite the PLL configuration. If multiple generated clocks exist on one node (mux scenario), show each with -add and the corresponding -master_clock, and justify with set_case_analysis where a static select is known.
signoff_risk: A mis-modeled generated clock causes the entire clock domain to be analyzed incorrectly. If the generated clock is treated as too fast (wrong multiply/divide), setup violations are missed → silicon timing failure on that domain. If treated as too slow, the domain over-optimizes → power/area waste, and hold violations may be introduced by excessive buffering. At advanced nodes, a wrong generated-clock phase can create millions of false violations that obscure real ones, or hide real violations behind a wrongly relaxed check.

pattern_name: False path vs multicycle path decision for intentional multi-cycle logic
situation: A data path is intentionally allowed N cycles to propagate (slow enable register, pipelined computation, divided-clock domain crossing, memory write data). The designer must choose between set_false_path (ignore entirely) and set_multicycle_path (relax to N cycles).
derivation: Use set_multicycle_path, never set_false_path, when the path is functionally real and simply takes N cycles. The canonical form: set_multicycle_path N -setup -from src -to dst; set_multicycle_path N-1 -hold -from src -to dst. The setup exception moves the capture edge to the Nth clock; the hold exception moves the hold check to the (N-1)th edge to prevent over-constraining hold. For a 2-cycle path: setup is checked at 2T, hold at 1T. The arithmetic: setup required time = launch_edge + NT − clock_uncertainty − T_setup; hold required time = launch_edge + (N-1)T + clock_uncertainty + T_hold. Forgetting the -hold counterpart leaves hold checked at 0T, which over-constrains and can create spurious hold violations, or conversely mask real ones. set_false_path is only correct when the path can NEVER be exercised (mutually exclusive mux selections, static test-mode configuration, asynchronous reset). Use false path to disable analysis entirely, multicycle to reschedule it.
wrong_way: Using set_false_path on a path that is actually a multicycle path. This silences all timing feedback — the implementation tool feels free to make the path arbitrarily slow, and the data may not be ready when the destination captures it N cycles later → intermittent silicon failure that is nearly impossible to debug. Conversely, using set_multicycle_path without the paired -hold exception: hold is checked at the wrong edge, producing either false hold violations (over-constraint) or missed hold bugs (under-constraint). A third error: applying multicycle with -end vs -start incorrectly for cross-clock domains, shifting the wrong clock's edge and arriving at an unintended capture relationship.
defense: Justify with the RTL: show that the data is explicitly enabled/staged such that it is valid N cycles after launch. For a multicycle path, prove that the destination enable is de-asserted for N-1 cycles after the source launches. For a false path, prove the two endpoints can never be active in the same functional mode (e.g., mux select is mutually exclusive, test mode is static). Formal verification of the exception assumption is increasingly required in mature flows.
signoff_risk: If the path is a real multicycle but was false-pathed: setup is never checked, so the tool may implement a path slower than N cycles → silicon data corruption that manifests as rare, unreproducible bugs. If the multicycle is missing its -hold counterpart: hold violations appear that are artifacts of the constraint error (over-constraint), wasting ECO effort; or hold is masked (under-constraint) → silicon hold failure. These are among the most dangerous SDC errors because they pass STA cleanly yet fail in silicon.

situation: A signal crosses from one clock domain to another, handled by a synchronizer chain (2-flop or more), handshake, or FIFO. STA must not treat it as a single-cycle timed path, but the precise treatment depends on the synchronizer type.
derivation: For a 2-flop synchronizer, the standard practice is set_false_path -from [get_clocks clk_a] -to [get_clocks clk_b] to suppress the cross-domain timing check, because the first flop of the synchronizer can go metastable and its exact timing relationship to clk_b is non-deterministic. However, modern methodology prefers a more graded approach: set_max_delay to bound the maximum propagation time (limiting metastability window) combined with set_min_delay to ensure the signal does not arrive too fast (which can cause the second flop of the synchronizer to see an illegal transition). A typical constraint: set_max_delay [expr 0.8  $period_b] -from [get_clocks clk_a] -to [get_clocks clk_b]; set_min_delay 0.5 -from …. This bounds the metastability window while preserving a meaningful timing check. For handshake/FIFO-based CDCs, false-path between the two domains is appropriate because the data is only valid when the handshake is asserted, which is itself a multi-cycle event. Pair the constraint with a set_case_analysis on the synchronizer's control signals if the synchronizer is only active in certain modes.
wrong_way: Timing the CDC path as a normal single-cycle path: the tool attempts to meet a clock-to-clock relationship that is physically meaningless, producing massive violation counts and forcing the implementation tool to waste effort optimizing a path that is architecturally a synchronizer. Conversely, blindly false-pathing ALL cross-domain paths: this can accidentally cover data paths that DO have a deterministic relationship (e.g., a clock divider producing a known phase relationship), hiding real timing problems. Another error: false-pathing only one direction (clk_a→clk_b) but not the reverse when the interface is bidirectional, leaving one direction unconstrained.
defense: Show the synchronizer structure in the RTL and prove that the first flop's output is allowed to go metastable. Justify false path or max/min delay with the synchronizer's MTBF calculation — the max_delay value should reflect the acceptable metastability window for the target MTBF. For handshake/FIFO CDCs, show that data is qualified by a request/acknowledge and that the false path is only on the raw data, not the handshake signals themselves.
signoff_risk: Over-constraining (no exception): the design cannot close timing on paths that are architecturally exempt, forcing wasteful optimization or an outright frequency reduction. Under-constraining (false path on a path that should be timed): the synchronizer's first flop may resolve too slowly, exceeding the MTBF budget → intermittent metastability failures in silicon that are temperature/voltage dependent and extremely hard to reproduce. At signoff, CDC mistakes are a leading cause of chips that 'work on the bench but fail in the field'.

situation: During early implementation (before CTS, before routing, before final parasitics), the design is optimized against an overly pessimistic view of the world. The engineer must decide how much margin to embed in the constraints and when to relax it.
derivation: Start with conservative margins: add extra clock uncertainty (e.g., 200-300 ps beyond jitter to model pre-CTS skew estimation error), use worst-case process corner, and possibly over-constrain I/O with smaller input/output delays (reserve more external budget). As the design matures: after CTS, replace estimated clock latency with set_propagated_clock and reduce clock_uncertainty to jitter-only (typically 50-100 ps). After routing, switch to extracted parasitics and apply derating. The key arithmetic: initial uncertainty = jitter + estimated_skew + guardband; final uncertainty = jitter only. If initial uncertainty was 250 ps and final is 80 ps, the design gains 170 ps of slack at signoff — but if the design barely closed under the optimistic final constraints, any process variation at silicon will cause failures. The disciplined approach: carry a guardband through to signoff. Never relax all the way to zero margin. A reasonable staged plan: pre-CTS uncertainty 0.25 ns, post-CTS 0.12 ns, post-route with real corners 0.08 ns + OCV derating.
wrong_way: Carrying the pessimistic early constraints all the way to signoff — the design is over-optimized (area, power penalty) and the team never discovers they could have run faster. Or the opposite: aggressively relaxing constraints at each stage and removing all guardband, so the design 'meets timing' in STA but has zero margin against process variation → systematic yield loss or temperature-dependent field failures. A third error: relaxing uncertainty but forgetting to switch from ideal to propagated clocks, or forgetting to enable OCV/AOCV/POCV derating — STA reports artificially rosy slack.
defense: Present a constraint versioning table: each stage (RTL, pre-CTS, post-CTS, post-route, signoff) with its uncertainty, latency model, and derating. Show that the final signoff constraints include appropriate guardband (typically 5-10% of period or a fixed 50-100 ps) atop pure jitter. Demonstrate that the design closes not just at nominal but across required process/voltage/temperature corners.
signoff_risk: Too much permanent margin: the chip ships at a lower frequency than achievable, leaving performance on the table and potentially losing market competitiveness. Too little margin: the chip passes STA but fails at silicon across PVT — a yield disaster that may require a respin. The art is in knowing how much guardband is 'enough' for the process node and market; at advanced nodes (<7nm), variation is higher and the guardband must be correspondingly larger.

pattern_name: Asynchronous interface input/output delay with board-level budget
situation: A source-synchronous or system-synchronous interface to an external device (DDR, LPDDR, high-speed serdes) where the data and clock relationships are governed by the board and the external device datasheet, not by internal clock trees.
derivation: Derive set_input_delay and set_output_delay from the external device datasheet and board trace delays. For a source-synchronous input: the clock and data arrive together from the external device. set_input_delay -max = Tco_max + board_trace_max − board_clock_trace_min; set_input_delay -min = Tco_min + board_trace_min − board_clock_trace_max. For a source-synchronous output: set_output_delay -max = downstream_Tsu + board_trace_max − board_clock_trace_min; set_output_delay -min = -(downstream_Thd - (board_clock_trace_max - board_trace_min)) where the negative value models the fact that data can leave after the clock. The key arithmetic: the sum of input_delay + internal delay + output_delay must fit within the available window dictated by the external device's access time and the clock period. For DDR, constraints must be applied to both clock edges (-clock_fall -add_delay). For LPDDR, Read and Write may use different virtual clocks to model the DQS relationship. Always pair -max and -min; omitting -min leaves hold unconstrained.
wrong_way: Using a simplistic percentage of the period (e.g., 40%) without consulting the external device datasheet. The real board delays may be much larger or smaller, making the constraint wrong by hundreds of picoseconds. Another error: neglecting the difference between clock trace length and data trace length on the board — this skew must be modeled in the -min/-max values. Forgetting -add_delay on DDR interfaces: the second constraint overrides the first, leaving one edge unconstrained. Treating a source-synchronous interface as system-synchronous (or vice versa) inverts the delay polarity, causing hold failures.
defense: Bring the external device datasheet: show Tco, Tsu, Thd, and the board stack-up with trace length estimates. Compute the input/output delay min/max from these numbers, accounting for board trace skew. For DDR, present the eye diagram showing both edges constrained. For LPDDR, show separate Read (DQS-centered) and Write (DQS-aligned) timing budgets.
signoff_risk: Too tight: the I/O cells and internal logic are over-optimized, costing area and power; the interface may still fail to close at the desired frequency. Too loose: at silicon, the external device misses setup or hold — the interface is flaky or dead. This class of error is especially nasty because it may pass STA but fail on the board due to the optimistic board-model assumptions baked into the virtual clock. At signoff, these interface failures are among the most expensive because they require board re-spins or chip frequency reductions after tapeout.

pattern_name: Reset and static configuration false-path derivation
situation: Asynchronous reset networks, scan-enable mux selects, boot-time configuration registers, and JTAG paths are topologically present but functionally never race against the clock in normal operation.
derivation: Apply set_false_path surgically: set_false_path -from [get_ports async_reset]; set_false_path -through [get_pins scan_mux/SEL]; set_false_path -from [get_cells config_reg]. The key discipline: scope the false path as narrowly as possible — only the specific ports/cells/pins that are truly static. For a scan enable mux, false-path only through the select pin, not through the entire mux, so data paths that mux between functional and scan sources remain timed. For a configuration register written once at boot, false-path -from the register's output, because after boot it becomes static. Pair with set_case_analysis where a signal is truly constant in a given mode (e.g., set_case_analysis 0 [get_ports scan_mode] in functional mode). The general rule: false path removes the timing check; set_case_analysis removes a logic state from analysis. Use both where appropriate.
wrong_way: Wildcard false-pathing (set_false_path -from [get_cells *]) which accidentally covers real timing paths. Or false-pathing an entire clock domain that contains both static and dynamic paths. Another error: using set_false_path on a reset that is actually synchronous in some modes — the reset deassertion timing matters and must be checked. A third error: false-pathing scan-related paths in the functional SDC but forgetting to re-enable them in the DFT SDC, so scan timing is never verified.
defense: In review, list every false path with its specific scope and the architectural reason (e.g., 'async_reset: reset is asynchronous, deassertion is synchronized externally; no single-cycle timing relationship'). Show that the scope is minimal — only the intended static signal. For scan paths, show the companion DFT constraint file that DOES time these paths. Use CDC verification tools to confirm the false path assumption holds against the RTL.
signoff_risk: Too broad: real functional paths are excluded from timing → silicon failure on those paths. Too narrow: false-path-worthy paths remain timed, generating spurious violations that consume implementation effort and may force the tool to over-optimize, costing area/power. In the worst case, a missing false path on a truly static signal causes the tool to report impossible violations that can only be waived late, after extensive wasted optimization effort. After an ECO, stale false paths are a notorious source of escaped bugs.
